§0 Where this lecture sits

Lecture 3 built graphs from data and measured them: their dimension, their curvature, their archetypes (cliques, grids, trees). Lecture 4 asks the question that the rest of machine learning asks next: can we learn on these structures the way convolutional networks learn on images? The answer of the slides is deliberately sober. The title of the first part is “Geometric deep learning is not a mature field” (p. 10): message passing generalises convolutions to graphs (p. 20), but five problems appear at once (p. 23–27), and the published benchmarks are often too easy or taken out of context (p. 35–38).

The second part is the author’s own experience with two projects: protein surfaces (MaSIF, then dMaSIF, p. 41–48) and lung registration, where a plain optimal transport solver with smoothing beats many deep networks (p. 49–56). The third part asks whether the graph itself should be learned: dynamic graphs, autoencoders and attention, which the slides write as a Nadaraya–Watson interpolator (p. 58–62). The lecture ends with the limits of “learning everything” and with advice on careers (p. 63–72).

Much of this lecture is argument rather than mathematics. This page turns each claim that can be measured into a lab, and keeps the others as clearly labelled opinions.

Threads of the course

The same seven threads are used on every companion page. A filled dot marks a lecture where the thread is central; a ring marks a lecture where it appears in passing. In the L4 column, each dot links to a section of this page; in the L1–L3 and L5–L7 columns, to those companions.

central in passingoutlined dots = this lecturehover or focus a dot for its content

This lecture’s stations. Four threads are central. Local → global: message passing is the local rule, and bottlenecks decide what reaches far away (§1.2, §1.6). Symmetry & curvature: a graph has no preferred direction, and a sphere cannot even be combed (§1.4); MaSIF builds rotation invariance into its surface features (§2.1). Honest models & baselines: benchmarks, incentives and a simple optimal transport solver that beats many networks (§1.8, §1.9, §2.4). Scale & computation: why irregular memory access slows graphs down, and a speed-up of several hundred times on protein surfaces (§1.7, §2.1). Three appear in passing: the recap of the curse of dimensionality (P.1), similarity learned in feature space by attention (§3.2), and meshes that sample the same surface differently (§1.5).

A question that comes back

What would a simple baseline do here?

The slides ask it about benchmarks: results on Graph-MNIST look promising “until you remember that test accuracy for basic K-NN classifiers on MNIST is 95%–99%” (p. 35), and “Keep track of both classical and learning-based baselines” (p. 39). This page asks it everywhere. A nearest-neighbour vote on raw pixels, trained on a twelfth of MNIST, rivals the graph networks of p. 35 (Lab 6). A parabola with three parameters extrapolates a cannonball where a ReLU network cannot (Lab 11). An optimal transport solver with smoothing, with no training at all, registers trees of vessels (Lab 8). And sometimes the baseline tells us that the claim is right: isotropic message passing really cannot detect an oriented edge (Lab 1).

Earlier lectures. Lecture 1 asked what a model should keep and what it should throw away; Lecture 2, what a model assumes where there is no data; Lecture 3, what can be learned from the neighbours alone. Here the model is a network whose layers pass messages between neighbours, and the question is whether that extra machinery beats what the earlier lectures already offered. Later lectures supply stronger baselines: geodesics on curved spaces (L5), optimal transport between distributions (L6), and code that makes such geometric methods fast (L7).

Prologue — from graphs to learning p. 1–9 · fr. 1–9

P.1 Recap: graphs and their archetypes p. 2–5 · fr. 2–5

What Lecture 3 established (p. 2). “Curse of dimensionality ⟹ Statistics on white noise is hopeless. We must understand the intrinsic structure of our data, even when it is embedded in a high-dimensional space of features. We may need to unwrap the manifold of plausible data samples.” In dimension 100, independent noise puts every sample at almost the same distance from every other one (L3 Lab 3), so a model can only learn if the data have a structure of much lower dimension.

Local and global (p. 3). “The K-NN graph describes the local structure of a dataset. Untangling a soup of edges to produce a global understanding is hard.” Lecture 3 measured both halves: shortest paths in a K-NN graph recover distances along a swiss roll, until a single edge short-circuits two layers (L3 Lab 5).

Three archetypes (p. 4–5). “Cliques are like balls with positive curvature. Grids are like planes with flat curvature. Trees are like saddles with negative curvature.” The pictures are those of Lecture 3: a clique of 10 vertices, a 3 × 3 piece of an infinite grid, a small tree (a centre of degree 3 whose three children have three leaves each), and the plastic toys with 5, 6 and 7 triangles around each vertex. Lecture 3 measured the analogy in two ways. The number of vertices within distance r of a vertex plateaus in a clique, grows like r² in a grid and like 2r in a binary tree (L3 Lab 7). The Ollivier–Ricci curvature of an edge is +1 in a clique, 0 in a grid and −½ in a 3-regular tree; the toys with 5, 6 and 7 triangles per vertex give +⅓, 0 and −¼ (L3 Lab 10).

Why the archetypes matter for learning. A convolutional network is designed for the middle case, the grid. The rest of the lecture keeps meeting the two other cases. A clique has no scale and cannot be downsampled (§1.6). A tree, or any graph with a narrow bridge, squeezes the information of many vertices through a few edges (§1.6, Lab 4). The citation on p. 4, Topping et al. (2021), is the paper that links these bottlenecks to negative curvature.

P.2 Embeddings as diagnostic tools p. 6 · fr. 6

The slide (p. 6). “Embedding methods such as UMAP are excellent diagnostic tools.” Two pictures. The first visualises “the set of integer numbers 1, 2, 3, …, 8,000,000” (from John Williamson’s blog post “What do numbers look like?”, [Wil]): each integer is described by its prime factors, and UMAP draws integers with similar factorisations close together. The second visualises “the differentiation of Hematopoietic stem cells”, from the “Liver, Week 7” to the “Bone marrow, Week 20”.

What the second picture is. The slide gives no source. The lecture folder contains the author’s working files, “DBSCAN L07 viewed in UMAP” and “DBSCAN BM20 viewed in UMAP” (not shown in the deck): eight clusters found by DBSCAN, coloured and displayed in the plane computed by UMAP, for week-7 liver cells (L07) and week-20 bone-marrow cells (BM20). The picture is therefore an embedding of single cells, with clusters computed separately and displayed on top.

Diagnostic, not proof. A diagnostic tool shows where to look; it does not measure. L3 §4 explained how UMAP works: a fuzzy K-NN graph, then a layout that keeps neighbours close and pushes the rest away. It also measured what such a layout keeps. On handwritten digits, UMAP scored 0.990 on trustworthiness, a score that would be 1 if no point had a false neighbour in the picture. But only neighbourhoods are kept: the sizes of clusters and the distances between them are not meaningful. Lab 9 uses UMAP again, as a representation whose K-NN graph can be compared with others.

P.3 Convolutional networks, three levels of description, and the plan p. 7–9 · fr. 7–9

The model to generalise (p. 7). “Since 2012, we have grown used to convolutional neural networks [PMC11].” The figure is Lecture 1’s LeNet-style network: a 32 × 32 input, 5 × 5 convolutions giving 28 × 28 feature maps, 2 × 2 subsampling to 14 × 14, a second convolution to 10 × 10, subsampling to 5 × 5, then fully connected layers that output one of the ten digits. The architecture dates from the late 1980s; 2012 is the year a much larger network of the same kind, trained on GPUs, won the ImageNet challenge, after which convolutional networks became the default for images. L1 §2.3 described them as a data-driven codec, reliable for textures and unreliable for high-level decisions.

The question of the lecture (p. 8). “Can we apply this methodology to higher-level descriptions?” The heart picture of L1 §1.2 shows three levels: 1. pixels, 2. anatomy (a contour or a mesh), 3. function (a graph of physical parameters). “Simplifying a bit, each level of analysis corresponds to a way of grouping pixels with their neighbors.” A convolution groups a pixel with the pixels of a small square. A mesh groups a vertex with the vertices of its triangles. A physical model groups the parts of an organ that interact. Geometric deep learning is the attempt to keep the recipe of CNNs (local, shared, stacked operations) when the neighbourhoods are no longer squares.

The plan (p. 9). “1. Geometric deep learning is not a mature field: convolutions on graphs and point clouds; a stimulating environment; questionable benchmarks. 2. Personal experience feedback: protein docking; lung registration. 3. Trying to learn a graph structure: dynamic graphs, auto-encoders and transformers; a continuous spectrum of models and jobs.” The page follows these three parts as §1, §2 and §3.

§1 Geometric deep learning is not a mature field p. 10–39 · fr. 10–31

§1.1 What is a convolution? p. 11–19 · fr. 10–11

The definition (p. 11–18). “Convolution (i.e. weighted average of the neighboring pixels): Cheap generalization of the product ‘a · x’, parameterized by the coefficients of a small filter φ.” The eight overlays are Lecture 1’s: the identity, three blurs, a horizontal derivative (shown signed, then as an absolute value), a vertical and a diagonal derivative. L1 Lab 9 recovered the eight 5 × 5 filters from the slide images and reproduced the outputs to within one grey level.

Why convolutions work so well on grids (p. 19). “Convolutions on grids: Are cheap. Enable pattern detection and texture analysis. Proven track record since the 1960’s: Gaussian blur, edge detectors, Laplacian pyramids, wavelets, JPEG2000, convolutional neural networks…” Three properties explain the success.

  • Few parameters. A 5 × 5 filter has 25 coefficients whatever the size of the image. A fully connected layer from a 54 × 54 image to another would have 544 ≈ 8.5 million.
  • Shared weights. The same coefficients are used at every pixel, so a pattern learned in one place is detected everywhere. In mathematical terms, the operation commutes with translations: shifting the image shifts the output.
  • A direction. Each coefficient is attached to an offset: “one pixel to the left” is not “one pixel up”. This is what lets filter 5 respond to vertical edges and filter 7 to horizontal ones.

The third property is easy to take for granted on a grid. §1.2 shows that it is the first one lost on a graph.

§1.2 Message passing on graphs p. 20 · fr. 12

Two formulas side by side (p. 20). On the left, a digit of MNIST with a 3 × 3 window; on the right, the same digit as a graph of superpixels, from the benchmark paper of Dwivedi et al. (2020). The slide writes the two operations with the same notation:

\[ \text{x}[\text{i},\text{j}] \;\gets\; \sum_{\text{k},\text{l}} \SIM{\varphi[\text{k},\text{l}]}\,\cdot\,\text{x}[\text{i}-\text{k},\,\text{j}-\text{l}] \qquad\qquad \text{x}[\text{i}] \;\gets\; \sum_{\text{i}\leftrightarrow\text{k}} \SIM{\varphi\big(}\,\text{x}[\text{i}],\,\text{x}[\text{k}],\,\SIM{\edge[\text{i},\text{k}]\,\big)} \]
\[ \text{x}[\text{i},\text{j}] \;\gets\; \sum_{\text{k},\text{l}} \SIM{\varphi[\text{k},\text{l}]}\,\cdot\,\text{x}[\text{i}-\text{k},\,\text{j}-\text{l}] \]
\[ \text{x}[\text{i}] \;\gets\; \sum_{\text{i}\leftrightarrow\text{k}} \SIM{\varphi\big(}\,\text{x}[\text{i}],\,\text{x}[\text{k}],\,\SIM{\edge[\text{i},\text{k}]\,\big)} \]

On the left, each pixel receives the values of its neighbours, weighted by a coefficient that depends on the offset (k, l). On the right, each vertex i receives a message φ(x[i], x[k], edge[i, k]) from each neighbour k, and adds them up. Stacking such layers, with non-linearities in between, gives a graph neural network.

A grid convolution is a special case. Take the graph whose vertices are the pixels, with an edge between pixels less than two rows and two columns apart, and let edge[i, k] be the offset from i to k. The message φ = φ[offset] · x[k] gives back the convolution exactly. Lab 1 checks it on the slide’s CT image: the two computations agree to the last bit.

What is lost when the edge carries no direction. On a general graph there is no natural “left” or “up”, so most graph layers use messages that depend on x[k] only, or on x[i] and x[k]: the same weight for every neighbour. Whatever the number of layers, the result can only depend on the graph distance and on how many paths lead from one vertex to another. On a grid, such a filter is invariant under the eight symmetries of the square (quarter turns and mirrors): it is isotropic. It can blur, and it can respond to blobs and rings, but it cannot tell a vertical edge from a horizontal one. Problem 1 of the slides (§1.4) says exactly this.

Lab 1

Convolutions as message passing, and what isotropic filters miss (p. 11–20, 23)

Question. A convolution is message passing with a weight per direction. If the weights cannot depend on the direction, how well can a graph network still imitate the slide’s eight filters?

The filter drawn on p. 23: weights that depend on the graph distance only
Its output on the same image (grey = 0)
What the lab shows (default: the horizontal derivative, 4 layers)
  • A convolution is message passing. Written as a sum of messages φ(edge[i, k]) · x[k] over the 25 neighbours of each pixel, with the offset as the edge feature, the slide’s eight filters give exactly the same images as the convolution: the largest difference is 0.
  • Isotropic filters reproduce the blurs. Two layers of vanilla message passing (the sum over the 4 neighbours, iterated) already reproduce the three blurs with R² ≥ 0.998, and four layers with R² ≥ 0.9999.
  • They cannot see edges. For the four derivative filters, the best isotropic imitation explains less than 0.5% of the variance (R² ≤ 0.0042), with 1 to 8 layers, with the rings of p. 23, and even with every 5 × 5 kernel that has the symmetries of the square. A symmetric filter gives the same response to a left-to-right and a right-to-left edge, so it cannot compute their difference.
  • Isotropic means rotation-proof. Rotating the image by a quarter turn and then applying the ring filter of p. 23 gives the same result as the reverse order, up to 1.4×10⁻¹²; for the horizontal derivative the two orders differ by up to 444 grey levels. Lack of orientation is the price of this invariance.

§1.3 Multiscale architectures on graphs p. 21 · fr. 13

The slide (p. 21). Left: “Grid convolutions + downsamplings”, Lecture 1’s wavelet cascade (x ⋆ φj−1, x ⋆ φj, x ⋆ φj+1: micro, meso, macro scales). Right: “Graph convolutions + downsamplings”, a figure from Bronstein et al. (2021) with four stages: an equivariant layer, a local pooling layer, another equivariant layer and an invariant global pooling that outputs one value for the whole graph.

Why multiscale matters. A 3 × 3 filter only sees one pixel away. After each 2 × 2 downsampling, the next filter sees twice as far in the original image. With five levels, a network with 3 × 3 filters sees the whole of a 64 × 64 image. On a grid, downsampling is canonical: keep one pixel in four. On a graph there is no canonical choice. The usual answer is graph coarsening: merge pairs of adjacent vertices, as in the Graclus algorithm, and connect the merged vertices when any of their members were connected. Lab 4 coarsens a grid, a clique and the bottleneck graph of p. 25 this way. The grid behaves like an image, with its diameter roughly halved at each level; the clique has diameter 1 at every level, so pooling it builds no hierarchy of scales.

§1.4 The promises, and problem 1: the lack of orientation p. 22–23 · fr. 14–15

The promise (p. 22). “We intend to leverage the intrinsic structure of: Point clouds. Surface and volume meshes. Molecular graphs, proteins. Social and communication networks. Unfortunately, things are not that simple.” Five problems follow, one per slide.

Problem 1 (p. 23). “How do we deal with the lack of orientation? CNNs learn oriented curve detectors. Vanilla graph convolutions define isotropic filters. Hairy ball theorem: no globally consistent 2D coordinates on a sphere.” The left picture comes from the Distill article on curve detectors (Cammarata et al. 2020): units of an image network that respond to curves at ten orientations. The middle picture, radial_filter.svg, is a 9 × 9 grid graph whose vertices are shaded by their graph distance to the centre: pale at distance 0, medium at distance 1, strongest at distance 2 (8 vertices), pale again at distance 3, white beyond. It is a ring detector that cannot prefer any direction; Lab 1 applies it to the CT image.

Why not simply add directions? On a mesh, one could attach to each vertex a reference direction in its tangent plane (“east”) and measure angles from it, as a CNN measures offsets on a grid. For this to work, the reference directions must vary continuously across the surface. On a sphere this is impossible. The hairy ball theorem states that every continuous tangent vector field on a sphere vanishes somewhere: you cannot comb a hairy ball flat without leaving a whorl, like the crown of the baby’s head on the slide.

A counting rule behind the theorem. Around each isolated zero of a field, walk once around a small loop and count how many turns the vector makes: this integer is the index of the zero (+1 for a source, a sink or a vortex, −1 for a saddle). The Poincaré–Hopf theorem says that on a closed surface, the indices of the zeros of any field add up to the Euler characteristic χ = V − E + F of the surface: 2 for a sphere, 0 for a torus. Since 2 ≠ 0, a sphere cannot carry a field without zeros; a torus can. Lab 2 finds the zeros of several fields on a triangulated sphere and torus, and adds up their indices.

Lab 2

Combing a hairy ball (p. 23)

Question. Can a field of “reference directions” cover a sphere without a singular point? What do all the fields we try have in common?

What the lab shows
  • No field on the sphere escapes. The rotation field has two zeros of index +1 (a vortex at each pole), the gradient of the height a source and a sink (+1, +1), and the “dipole” a single zero of index +2. Twenty random smooth fields have between 2 and 8 zeros each, some of index −1 (saddles). In every case the indices add up to 2 = V − E + F for the triangulated sphere (2,562 − 7,680 + 5,120).
  • The torus can be combed. The field along the tube has no zero at all. The gradient of a height has a maximum, a minimum and two saddles (+1 +1 −1 −1), and the random fields have 4 to 12 zeros; the indices always add up to 0 = V − E + F.
  • What it means for learning. A convolution on a surface that measures angles from a “reference direction” needs such a field. On a sphere, or any surface of the same shape as a protein or an organ, the field must break down somewhere, and the filter responses jump around those points. This is why MaSIF takes the best of several rotations of its filters (§2.1).
Link

How do methods on surfaces live with the theorem? MaSIF (§2.1) computes its filters in polar coordinates around each point and takes the maximum over K rotations of the filter, so that the arbitrary choice of the angular origin does not matter (p. 44). Gauge-equivariant networks, the “gauges” of the title of Bronstein et al. (2021), instead transform the features consistently when the reference direction changes. Both accept the lesson of the hairy ball: there is no global “east” on a sphere. The same Euler characteristic that counts zeros here also totals the angle deficits of a closed mesh in L3 Lab 9 (4π for a sphere, 0 for a torus).

§1.5 Problem 2: varying sampling densities p. 24 · fr. 16

The slide (p. 24). “How do we deal with varying sampling densities? MRI slice: voxel size = 1 mm³. ‘Hell is other people’s meshes’ – Jean-Paul Sartre. Intrinsic triangulations. Can we use them for ML?” An image comes with a sampling chosen once and for all by the scanner, known and regular. A mesh or a point cloud comes with whatever sampling its author chose: long thin triangles on a CAD model, dense regions where the scanner lingered. The joke on Sartre (“Hell is other people”, Huis clos) says that other people’s meshes are rarely the ones you would have made. Intrinsic triangulations (Sharp, Soliman and Crane 2019, [SSC19]) keep the surface fixed and improve its triangles along the surface itself, without moving any vertex off it.

What goes wrong for a network. A vanilla graph layer only sees the graph: who is connected to whom. Move the vertices of a mesh without changing its triangles, and the graph is unchanged, so the layer computes exactly the same thing, although the surface it describes has changed. Conversely, the same surface meshed twice gives two different graphs, and two different answers. A method that should depend on the surface must use the geometry of the mesh (lengths, angles, areas), not just its connectivity.

The fix used in geometry processing. The cotangent Laplacian weights each edge by (cot α + cot β)/2, where α and β are the two angles facing the edge, and the lumped mass matrix gives each vertex a third of the area of its triangles. Together they discretise the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the surface itself, the same operator whichever triangulation is used, which is why DiffusionNet (Sharp et al. 2022, L3 p. 29) learns with heat diffusion built from them. Lab 3 diffuses heat on one flat square meshed three ways.

Lab 3

One surface, three samplings (p. 24)

Question. The same bump of heat spreads on a flat square for the same time. Does the result depend on how the square was meshed, and on which operator does the spreading?

Temperature after time t on the chosen mesh
Triangles drawn at their true positions; darker = hotter in the light theme, brighter in the dark theme.
Profile along the horizontal axis (y = 0)
What the lab shows (initial bump of width 0.08, heat equation for t = 0.01, lattice spacing 0.04)
  • The geometric operator does not care about the mesh. With the cotangent Laplacian and the mass matrix, the heat after time t matches the exact solution to within 0.34%, 0.41% and 0.38% (root-mean-square error, relative to the peak) on the uniform, graded and jittered meshes. The spread of the heat is 0.1625 in both directions on the uniform and graded meshes and 0.1624–0.1625 on the jittered one, as in the exact solution (0.1625).
  • Message passing depends on the mesh. The mean over the neighbours, repeated 50 times, was calibrated to match the exact solution on the uniform mesh (it does, to better than 0.01%). On the jittered mesh its error is 0.91%. On the graded mesh, where triangles at x = +0.6 are 2.6 times wider than at x = −0.6, the heat drifts towards the sparse side (its centre moves to x = 0.031) and spreads 34% too far horizontally (σx = 0.2185 instead of 0.1625): the error is 6.2%.
  • Why. Each step of message passing moves heat by one edge, whatever the length of the edge. Where the edges are longer, heat travels further in the same number of steps. The cotangent weights and the areas carry the missing information about lengths.
Watch out

The slide’s “voxel size = 1 mm³” is a round number, not a property of every MRI. Many clinical sequences, cardiac cine MRI among them, acquire thick slices (several millimetres) with finer pixels inside each slice, so their voxels are far from cubes. The point of the slide survives: an image’s sampling is known and regular, even when it is anisotropic, whereas a mesh’s sampling is whatever its author made it.

§1.6 Problem 3: highly non-Euclidean graphs p. 25 · fr. 17

The slide (p. 25). “How do we deal with highly non-Euclidean graphs? Downsampling a grid is easy. How do we downsample a clique? How do we handle bottlenecks?” The three pictures are the CT image and its version at half resolution, the clique of 10 vertices of p. 4, and two dense clusters joined by a single edge, drawn in blue among red ones: the colours encode curvature, as in the paper cited, Topping et al. (2021).

Over-squashing. After L layers, a vertex’s features depend on the vertices within L edges. In a tree or through a bridge, the number of such vertices grows fast, but all their information must pass through a few edges and be squeezed into a vector of fixed size. Topping et al. make this precise for message passing with the normalised adjacency matrix \(\hat{\text{A}} = \tilde{\text{D}}^{-1/2}(\text{A}+\text{I})\,\tilde{\text{D}}^{-1/2}\): the sensitivity of vertex i’s output to vertex j’s input, \(|\partial \text{h}_\text{i}^{(\text{L})} / \partial \text{x}_\text{j}|\), is bounded by a constant times \((\hat{\text{A}}^\text{L})_{\text{ij}}\), the weight of all paths of length L from j to i. For a linear network the bound is an equality. They then show that edges of very negative curvature are where this weight collapses, and propose to rewire the graph: add edges around the most negatively curved ones. The unused figure oversquashing.png in the lecture folder shows it: the same bottleneck graph before and after rewiring, and a dumbbell surface whose neck widens.

Lab 4

Bottlenecks, over-squashing and rewiring (p. 21, 25)

Question. How much does a vertex hear from the other side of the bridge after L layers, and how much do a few extra edges help? And what does pooling do to a grid, a clique and this graph?

The graph of p. 25, digitised: edges coloured by Ollivier–Ricci curvature, vertices by their sensitivity to the source
Mean sensitivity (ÂL)ij across the bridge and within the clusters
Pooling by heavy-edge matching (Graclus-style), four levels
What the lab shows (default: L = 4, no rewiring)
  • Curvature finds the bottleneck. The bridge has Ollivier–Ricci curvature −1.071; the next most negative edge is at −0.200, and the median edge is at +0.293. Only 5 of the 82 edges are negatively curved.
  • Little gets across. After 4 layers, a vertex receives on average 2.1×10⁻³ of the signal of a vertex on the other side of the bridge, against 6.2×10⁻² from its own cluster: 30 times less. More layers help slowly: the ratio is 85 after 1 layer, 30 after 4 and 16 after 8.
  • A few edges help a lot. Adding 6 edges around the most negatively curved edge, one at a time (a simplified version of Topping et al.’s rewiring), multiplies the sensitivity across by 4.9 (to 1.0×10⁻²) and brings the ratio down to 5.4, while the diameter drops from 7 to 6. The most negative curvature rises from −1.071 to −0.611.
  • Pooling a clique builds no scales. Pairing adjacent vertices (heavy-edge matching) turns the 8 × 8 grid into 33, 18, 10 and 6 vertices, with the diameter falling from 14 to 7, 5, 4 and 2, like downsampling an image. The clique of 10 keeps diameter 1 at every level (10, 5, 3, 2 vertices, then 1): every level sees the whole graph in one step, so there is nothing for a hierarchy to add.
Watch out

The slide’s graph has no data file; the lab uses a digitisation of bottleneck.png. The 30 vertices and 82 edges were read from the picture automatically, and 14 more candidate edges, which pass exactly behind a third vertex, were left out because the picture cannot tell a long edge from two short ones. The digitised graph is connected, has exactly one bridge between two clusters of 15 vertices, and the picture’s edge colours agree with the Ollivier–Ricci curvatures computed on it (correlation 0.76 between the edges’ redness and their curvature). Topping et al. colour edges with their own “balanced Forman” curvature, which the slide does not state.

§1.7 Problems 4 and 5: GPUs, and too many applications p. 26–27 · fr. 18–19

Problem 4 (p. 26). “GPUs are not optimized for graphs. Fixed + contiguous neighborhoods ⟹ Optimal compilation. Varying sizes + random memory accesses ⟹ ×100 slow-down.” The left drawing is a digit on a grid with a 5 × 5 window whose rows are highlighted: on a grid, the neighbours of a pixel lie in a few contiguous runs of memory. The right drawing is a 6-vertex graph: to update vertex 1, the processor must gather the features of vertices 2, 4 and 6 from wherever they are stored, add them up and write the result.

Why this matters on a GPU. A GPU runs threads in groups of 32 (a warp) that execute the same instruction together. When the 32 threads read 32 consecutive numbers, the hardware serves them with a few wide memory transactions; when they read 32 scattered numbers, it needs up to 32. When neighbourhoods have different sizes, the threads of a warp wait for the one with the most neighbours. And a grid convolution can load a tile of the image into fast on-chip memory once and reuse each value for all the filters that need it, which a gather over an arbitrary graph cannot plan for. Lab 5 counts these effects with a simple model of a GPU and times the gather on this computer’s processor.

Problem 5 (p. 27). “The range of target applications is too wide.” Molecules [Dil15], lidar scans [Lu19], social networks [Gra19]. Molecules have tens of atoms and chemical bonds with types; a lidar scan has millions of points and no edges at all; a social network has millions of vertices whose degrees range from one to millions. No single architecture, benchmark or software library serves all three well.

Lab 5

Why graphs are slow on GPUs: memory access patterns (p. 26)

Question. Where does the slow-down of p. 26 come from, and how much of it disappears if the vertices are simply stored in a better order?

Storage order of the vertices in a 16 × 16 corner (dark = stored first in the light theme)
GPU model: memory sectors read per warp, relative to perfectly contiguous reads
What the lab shows
  • A grid read in order is almost perfect. In the GPU model, a warp of 32 threads reading one float per neighbour touches 1.10 times as many 32-byte memory sectors as a perfectly contiguous read. Shuffling the storage order of the same grid makes it 6.59 times.
  • A K-NN graph is scattered by default. For the K-NN graph of random points, stored in the order the points were generated, the ratio is 6.65, and a 32 KB cache misses 77% of the reads. Sorting the vertices along a Z-order curve, so that points close in space are close in memory, brings these down to 2.29 and 0.8% (the advice of L7 §1.10, measured in L7 Lab 5).
  • Varying degrees waste threads. In the K-NN graph each vertex reads between 7 and 14 values (itself and its neighbours), so within a warp the threads with few neighbours wait for the one with the most: only 73.7% of the thread slots do useful work, against 100% on the grid.
  • More features per vertex hide the problem. With 8 or more floats per vertex (32 bytes), each neighbour fills whole sectors and the ratio falls to 1.00 for every order, or below when threads of a warp share neighbours (0.66 for the sorted K-NN graph). Real networks have 64 to 256 features per vertex; their remaining costs are the index array itself and the lack of reuse between neighbouring vertices, which a stencil gets for free.
  • On this computer’s processor (click the button), the gather through an index array is slower than the fixed-offset stencil even in the natural order, and slower still in shuffled order. The slide’s ×100 is a claim about GPUs, which a page running on the processor cannot measure; the model above shows where such factors come from.

§1.8 A community and its incentives p. 28–34 · fr. 20–26

A solution in search of a problem (p. 28–30). “In 2017, geometric deep learning was a solution in search of a problem.” It attracted computer scientists “looking for new ways of combining features”, mathematicians “looking for new applications of their insights” and domain experts “looking for a breakthrough on their data”. The literature grew fast: “Dozens of different convolution operators. Renewed interest in theoretical graph ML. Useful extensions for PyTorch: PyG, DGL, KeOps… Cross-pollination between different fields.” But “it is hard to recommend some methods over the others: Applications are wildly different from each other. Most theoretical and experimental works are proof-of-concepts. Benchmarks are highly unreliable.”

Science is not done in a vacuum (p. 31–33). The myth, in two paintings: Archimedes (“Don’t disturb my circles”) and Edelfelt’s portrait of Louis Pasteur (1885), “alone in the lab”. The reality, in two slides of the author’s observations about structural incentives. French mathematicians are judged on the “top 3 deepest ideas over a career”, which “promotes long-term, original thought” but gives “no incentives for outreach and interdisciplinary research”. INRIA researchers aim at “1 meaningful contribution every 5 years”. French hospital doctors are judged by their PubMed record, which drives MERRI research funding, hence an “inflation of low-quality papers”. In US and UK computer-science departments, universities “climb up the Shanghai ranking”, professors “maximize the hype” and are “allowed to take risks, but not allowed to fail”, and students take the “safest route: incremental research, claim SOTA every 6 months”.

The conclusion (p. 34). “Peer-reviewed ≠ Scientific truth. In the current ML community, relatively few actors are incentivized to: review papers carefully; document baselines thoroughly; admit that an idea doesn’t work; take the massive amount of time that is needed to make their experiments truly reproducible; keep the codebase up to date with a software stack that breaks every 6 months. ⟹ Unfortunately, the NeurIPS/ICML/… stamp means little. We cannot trust the conclusions of a paper without reproducing the experiments or checking the proofs carefully.”

Beyond the slides

Slides 32–33 are the author’s account of incentives, not measurements, and this page does not try to check them. The last one, p. 34, is a method that this page follows literally: each claim of the lecture that can be tested is tested in a lab, with the code in the reference implementations. The same rule caught two slips in the author’s own figures in earlier lectures (L2 §1.4, L3 §1.3).

§1.9 Benchmarks: sanity checks, saturation, and loss of context p. 35–39 · fr. 27–31

Nothing but a sanity check (p. 35). “Results on Graph-MNIST look promising… Until you remember that test accuracy for basic K-NN classifiers on MNIST is 95%–99%.” The table comes from Dwivedi et al. (2020): each MNIST digit becomes a graph of superpixels (figure above), and networks with about 100,000 parameters classify the graphs. The table’s own first row makes the point even more sharply than the caption: the MLP, which processes the superpixels without using the edges at all, scores 95.340%, above GCN (90.120%), “vanilla GCN” (90.705%) and MoNet (90.805%). The best graph networks, GatedGCN (97.340%) and GraphSage (97.312%), are two points above it.

What “basic K-NN” gives. A 1-nearest-neighbour vote on the raw pixels, with the plain Euclidean distance and no training at all, gives 96.91% on the 10,000 test images when it may search all 60,000 training images, and the 3-nearest-neighbour vote gives 97.05% (measured with the Python snippet 6). That is the low end of the slide’s range; the high end, 99%, needs a distance that tolerates small deformations of the digits. Lab 6 runs the vote in this page on a subset of MNIST.

Lab 6

A sanity check for Graph-MNIST (p. 20, 35, 63)

Question. How many training images does a nearest-neighbour vote need to match the graph networks of p. 35, and does turning images into superpixel graphs lose information?

Test accuracy of the vote against the number of training images (1,000 test images)
The table of p. 35 (Dwivedi et al. 2020, MNIST superpixels, 55,000 training graphs), with nearest-neighbour votes added
The first misclassified test images (label → vote)
What the lab shows (default: raw pixels, K = 1, 5,000 training images)
  • A vote with no training rivals the graph networks. With 5,000 training images, a 1-nearest-neighbour vote on raw pixels classifies 92.0% of the 1,000 test images correctly: better than GCN (90.120%), vanilla GCN (90.705%) and MoNet (90.805%) of p. 35, which were trained on 55,000 images. With all 60,000 training images the vote reaches 96.91% (3-NN: 97.05%), above 10 of the 12 rows of the table that report an accuracy, including the MLP, GAT and GIN; only GatedGCN (97.340%) and GraphSage (97.312%) remain above it.
  • The graph adds little. In the table itself, the MLP baseline of the paper, which ignores the edges, scores 95.34%, more than every GCN variant.
  • Superpixels keep the information. Replacing each image by its 81 superpixels (each region painted with its mean intensity) changes the 1-NN accuracy from 92.0% to 91.8%. Graph-MNIST is a harder way to present an easy problem.
  • Data are the real currency. With 50 training images the vote is right 61.6% of the time, with 500 79.9%, with 5,000 92.0%. This is problem 1 of p. 63 in numbers: a clinical dataset of 50 patients is on the left of this curve, not on the right.
Watch out

To keep this page light, it embeds the first 5,000 training images and every tenth test image of MNIST, each pixel reduced to 4 grey levels. The reduction costs about one point of accuracy: with the full 256 grey levels, the same 5,000 training images give 93.4% with a 1-nearest-neighbour vote on the same 1,000 test images, against 92.0% here (Python snippet 6). The numbers of the graph networks come from 55,000 training images; the fair comparison with them is the full-data vote, 96.91%.

Saturated benchmarks (p. 36). “Challenging large-scale benchmarks are published every year… But the review system pushes authors towards overfitting on ‘classic’ datasets.” The figure, from Rozenberszki, Litany and Dai (2022), compares ScanNet, a benchmark of indoor 3D scenes with 20 categories, with ScanNet200, which has 200 categories with a long tail of rare ones, as in real scenes.

Taken out of context (p. 37–38). The MPI FAUST dataset (Bogo et al. 2014) “contains 300 real-life scans of 10 subjects – 30 poses each. Problem: fit a reference mesh to the noisy 3D point clouds. Challenges: different topologies, missing data, self contacts. Dense ground truth correspondence for training = 10x10 meshes with identical topology.” Then: “The PyG library and many papers on graph neural networks discard the original point clouds to focus entirely on the 100 pre-aligned meshes. New problem: use (x, y, z) coordinates as input features for each node ⟹ predict node indices in [1, 6890] as output signal. Train on 80 surfaces, test on the remaining 20. Irrelevant to shape registration: we learn to overfit on the reference triangulation.”

Why the new problem is so much easier. The 100 meshes are fits of one template with 6,890 vertices, so every mesh has exactly the same triangles, stored in the same order. Vertex 1234 of a test mesh sits at the same place on the body as vertex 1234 of every training mesh, it has the same neighbours in the graph, and the answer to “which template vertex is this?” is its own position in the file. A graph network sees the identical connectivity in training and test; the meshes are also aligned in space. The real task, fitting the template to a raw scan with holes, noise, a different sampling and touching limbs, has none of these shortcuts. High scores on the simplified task say little about the real one.

How can we judge? (p. 39) “Keep track of both classical and learning-based baselines, in each application domain. This is time-consuming – focus on 2-3 subjects at most. It is likely that the wave of papers on geometric deep learning will fade in most applications settings, and stick in some productive niches: Shape analysis? Chemistry? Social sciences? This is how scientific progress takes place. The hype cycle is a normal and well-documented phenomenon.”

§2 Some personal experience p. 40–56 · fr. 32–47

§2.1 Protein surfaces: MaSIF and dMaSIF p. 41–46 · fr. 32–37

Two problems in structural biology (p. 41). “Folding and design”: predicting the 3D structure of a protein from its sequence of amino acids, and the reverse. “Docking – interacting surfaces”: predicting whether and how two proteins bind.

A physical prior (p. 42). “Docking is a function of the protein surfaces. Physical prior: no need to deal with the full volumes, we are looking for surface fingerprints.” The figure of MaSIF (Gainza et al. 2020) marks what a fingerprint contains: hydrophobic patches, electron donors, pockets, knobs, positive charges. The approach is a “systematic extraction of patches”, discs on the surface around many centre points.

Input features (p. 43). “We can compute geometric and chemical input features on local patches with ≃ 1 nm radius.” Geometric: the shape index and a distance-dependent curvature. Chemical: hydropathy, continuum electrostatics, free electrons and protons. (One nanometre is 10 ångströms; MaSIF uses patches of 9 Å and 12 Å geodesic radius.)

Geodesic patches (p. 44). Each patch is described in polar coordinates, a geodesic distance d and an angle θ, and mapped to a learned soft grid; convolution layers are applied for K rotations of the filters, and the result becomes a “fingerprint descriptor”. “Built-in invariance to 3D rotations, translations and the inner content of the protein. Enforces a locality prior: won’t overfit on scattered patterns.” Taking the best of K rotations is MaSIF’s answer to the problem of orientation (§1.4): the angle θ = 0 is an arbitrary choice at each point, so the result must not depend on it.

Applications (p. 45). “After training on the Protein Data Bank (with careful train-test split), this enables three tasks of interest”: classifying the pocket of a ligand (ADP, CoA, FAD, HEME, NAD, NADP, SAM), predicting interface sites, and ultra-fast search of interacting pairs.

dMaSIF (p. 46). “A proof-of-concept that has been received well”: MaSIF made the cover of Nature Methods (February 2020). The figure compares it with dMaSIF (Sverrisson, Feydy, Correia and Bronstein 2021). MaSIF computes a surface mesh (6 s), features (20 s) and patches (50 s) in a pre-processing stage, then runs its network (165 ms). dMaSIF works on the fly from the atoms: points and normals (70 ms), features (50 ms), local coordinates (6 ms), output (40 ms). “×100 - ×1,000 faster, lighter and fully differentiable.”

Key idea

dMaSIF’s surface is not a mesh but a level set. Around the atoms ak, with radii σk, define a smooth distance

\[ \text{SD}(\text{x}) \;=\; -\,\bar\sigma(\text{x})\,\log \sum_\text{k} \exp\!\Big(-\frac{\|\text{x}-\text{a}_\text{k}\|}{\sigma_\text{k}}\Big), \]
\[ \bar\sigma(\text{x}) \;=\; \frac{\sum_\text{k} \sigma_\text{k}\, e^{-\|\text{x}-\text{a}_\text{k}\|}}{\sum_\text{k} e^{-\|\text{x}-\text{a}_\text{k}\|}}, \]

a soft minimum of the distances to the atoms. The surface is the set where SD(x) = 1.05 Å. To sample it, throw random points around the atoms, move each one by a few steps of gradient descent on (SD − 1.05)², discard the points that got trapped inside, and keep one average point per cube of 1 Å. Normals are the gradient of SD. Curvatures come from a small least-squares fit of how the normals turn around each point. Everything is a formula of the atoms’ coordinates, so it can be differentiated and run on a GPU in milliseconds.

Lab 7

A protein surface from its atoms, after dMaSIF (p. 41–46)

Question. Can the surface fingerprint of a real protein be computed from its atoms in a browser, and are its features really invariant to rotations? Do the surfaces of two partners fit together?

Rotation test: the same atoms, rotated and shifted, then everything recomputed
Docking test: curvature of barnase against the facing point of barstar
What the lab shows (dMaSIF’s parameters: level 1.05 Å, 20 samples per atom, 1 Å cells, curvature scales 1–10 Å)
  • The recipe works in a browser. From the 864 heavy atoms of barnase, 17,280 random samples are drawn; 12,002 end up on the level set 1.05 Å and outside the protein; grouped into cubes of 1 Å they give 3,573 surface points with normals. The readout gives the computing time on your computer.
  • The features are rotation-invariant. Rotate and shift the atoms, and recompute everything: the new surface points are, after rotating back, a median 0.37 Å from the old ones (the random samples differ), and their curvatures agree with the old ones with correlations 0.977 (H), 0.977 (K) and 0.961 (shape index) at the 3 Å scale, and 0.984–0.987 for H and K at 5 Å. Raw coordinates do not: the x coordinate before and after correlates at −0.325.
  • The finest scale is the noisiest. At 1 Å the correlations drop to 0.92–0.93 for H and K and 0.84 for the shape index: a fingerprint at the scale of the sampling mostly records the sampling.
  • Partners have complementary shapes. At the 332 barnase points within 2 Å of barstar in the crystal, the mean curvature of barnase and that of the facing barstar point are anti-correlated, −0.41 at 1 Å and −0.48 at 2 Å (bumps face hollows), against about 0 for random pairs. The effect is weaker and irregular at larger scales (−0.13 at 3 Å, −0.34 at 5 Å, −0.07 at 10 Å), where both surfaces look convex: at 5 Å and 10 Å all of barnase’s mean curvatures are positive.
Watch out

“×100 - ×1,000 faster” compares different things. From atoms to output, MaSIF takes 6 + 20 + 50 s + 165 ms = 76.2 s and dMaSIF 70 + 50 + 6 + 40 ms = 166 ms: ×459, inside the slide’s range. But 76 of MaSIF’s seconds are pre-processing, done once per protein. When the surfaces of a dataset are computed in advance, the network itself runs in 165 ms against 40 + 6 ms for dMaSIF’s last two stages, about ×4. The ×459 is what matters when surfaces must be recomputed at every step, as when a protein is being designed or moved during docking, and it is what makes dMaSIF differentiable end to end.

§2.2 Is deep learning truly a revolution? Rosetta, and a recap p. 47–48 · fr. 38–39

Rosetta (p. 47). The timeline shows two decades of results of the Rosetta software for protein design, from the first structure predictions before 2000 to the de novo design of a β-barrel in 2018. The plot shows a docking energy landscape: the interface energy of candidate poses (kcal/mol) against their distance to the true pose (interface RMS, Å); the lowest energies sit near the true pose. Its energy is a weighted sum of terms, \(\text{E}_\text{total} = \sum_\text{i} \text{w}_\text{i}\, \text{E}_\text{i}(\Theta_\text{i}, \text{aa}_\text{i})\) (Alford et al. 2017), where each Ei is a physical potential (van der Waals attraction and repulsion, solvation, electrostatics, hydrogen bonds) or a statistical term learned from known structures, evaluated on the geometry Θi and amino acids aai, and the weights wi are fitted to data. “After 20 years of work, the developers of the Rosetta software have de facto developed a hybrid ‘point neural network’ that combines physical potentials with data-driven residuals.” Lab 11 builds such a hybrid in miniature: a physical law plus a small learned correction.

Recap on MaSIF and dMaSIF (p. 48). “Inspiring prototype that shows how far we can go if we drop complex physical terms but preserve the symmetries of the problem. With clever geometry and code, we can do interesting science on a single GPU. Nowhere near close to a finished product: maintaining software is a full-time job. Well-funded and mature fields already showcase formidable baselines. As outsiders, we can propose stimulating ideas and tools. Always stay humble – understanding the full context takes years.”

§2.3 Lung registration “Exhale – Inhale” p. 49–53 · fr. 40–44

The problem (p. 49). Given the tree of blood vessels of the lungs, extracted from a CT scan at full inhalation and at full exhalation, find where each point moved: “Complex deformations, high resolution (50k–300k points), high accuracy (< 1mm). Point clouds are more challenging than volumes, but robust to acquisition parameters.” This is registration, a problem the slides of Lecture 6 will write as minimising a distance between a deformable model and a fixed target.

Point neural networks (p. 50–51). PointPWC (Wu et al. 2020) is a multiscale network on point clouds: it computes descriptors of both clouds at several resolutions, from the full cloud down to a few dozen times fewer points, and at each scale matches them with a “cost volume” and refines a flow field, coarse to fine. “Point neural nets, in practice: compute descriptors at all scales; match them using geometric layers; train on synthetic deformations. Strengths and weaknesses: good at pairing branches; hard to train to high accuracy. ⟹ Complementary to geometric methods such as optimal transport.”

Three steps (p. 52–53). The method of Shen, Feydy et al. (NeurIPS 2021): 1. an affine pre-alignment by robust optimal transport (RobOT); 2. a deep network predicts a deformation, regularised by a smooth deformation model, trained end to end on synthetic pairs (real sources deformed by random local and global deformations); 3. a post-processing by robust optimal transport and splines. “This pragmatic method: is easy to train on synthetic data; scales up to high-resolution: 100k points in 1s; excellent results: KITTI (outdoors scans) and DirLab (lungs).”

Key idea

Optimal transport matches two clouds globally. Give each source point xi a mass 1/N and each target point yj a mass 1/M, and look for the transport plan π (how much mass goes from i to j) that minimises the total cost \(\sum_{\text{ij}} \pi_{\text{ij}}\, \|\text{x}_\text{i}-\text{y}_\text{j}\|^2/2\), with every source sending its mass and every target receiving its mass. Unlike “move each point to its nearest neighbour”, a plan cannot send the whole source to one attractive branch of the target: each target point can only absorb its share. The entropic version, solved by Sinkhorn iterations, blurs the plan at a scale ε (the “blur”), which makes it fast. The robust (unbalanced) version replaces the two mass constraints by penalties of strength ρ, so that points without a counterpart, such as a missing branch or outliers, may keep part of their mass instead of being forced onto something wrong. Each source point then moves to the barycentre of the targets it sends mass to, and a Gaussian smoothing of these displacements enforces a coherent deformation.

§2.4 An optimal transport baseline beats many networks p. 54–56 · fr. 45–47

The benchmark (p. 54). KITTI scene flow: pairs of 3D point clouds of street scenes a fraction of a second apart, computed from stereo images and their depth, with the ground-truth motion of every point: “3D scene flow estimation task, derived from a 2D + depth dataset. This is a standard (but maybe questionable) benchmark.” The figure shows cars (C1–C3), signs and ground patches in a 16 m × 16 m scene.

The result (p. 55). “Surprise: a baseline optimal transport solver with smoothing (RobOT) outperforms many deep learning methods on all metrics.” The table reports, for each method, the number of points, time, memory, and six accuracy metrics: the mean end-point error in 3D (EPE3D, cm), the shares of points with a strict and a relaxed accuracy (Acc3DS, Acc3DR), the share of outliers, and the same errors projected on the image (EPE2D, Acc2D). Lab 8 contains the whole table and lets you count, for any reference row, how many of the six metrics each other row beats.

Recap (p. 56). “Pragmatic approach: get the best of both data-driven and deterministic methods. Tables of numbers look impressive – but can hide critical information. Code base is not clean – top priority going forward. Evaluation on 3D scene flow is questionable. Shouldn’t we work with the original 2D data? Evaluation on medical data is hard: we release a new dataset of 1,000 pairs for training – without annotations. We only have access to 10 pairs with dense annotations for evaluation.” The ten annotated pairs are those of DirLab (Castillo et al. 2013, [CCF+13]).

Lab 8

Registration by optimal transport, after RobOT (p. 49–56)

Question. Without any training, how well do nearest neighbours, optimal transport and robust optimal transport register a deformed tree of vessels, and what do pre-alignment and smoothing add? And what exactly does the table of p. 55 say?

Source, target, and the source moved by the estimated flow (coloured by its error)
All methods on this target (errors in units of the picture, which is 2 wide)
What the lab shows (default: full target, robust optimal transport with pre-alignment, blur 0.02, σ = 0.05)
  • Nearest neighbours fail on vessels. Moving each source point to its nearest target point gives a mean end-point error (EPE) of 0.0606, almost as large as the true displacements themselves (0.0668 on average): 94.8% of the points are outliers. Neighbouring branches of the target attract the points of the wrong branch.
  • Optimal transport matches branches globally. Balanced optimal transport divides the error by 4.2 (EPE 0.0144); smoothing brings it to 0.0093, and an affine pre-alignment to 0.0086, with 95.6% of the points within the relaxed accuracy threshold. No training was involved.
  • Robustness has a price on complete data… Robust transport with the same pre-alignment and smoothing gives EPE 0.0128: when nothing is missing, allowing mass to stay behind throws away part of the information (93% of the mass is transported).
  • …and pays off when data are missing. When one branch is missing from the target and 10% of outliers are added, balanced transport becomes worse than nearest neighbours (EPE 0.0905 against 0.0609, on the points whose branch exists): it must send every bit of mass somewhere, including onto the outliers. Robust transport more than halves that error (0.0424), but the task stays hard: only 29.1% of the points reach the relaxed accuracy.
  • The table of p. 55, read row by row. RobOT with 30,000 points beats FlowNet3D, SPLATFlowNet, BCL, HPLFlowNet, FLOT and self-supervised PWC on all six metrics: “many deep learning methods on all metrics” is accurate. But supervised PWC at 8,000 points beats it on 3 metrics, and the three pipelines that combine networks with RobOT beat it on all 6. At equal resolution (8,000 points), raw RobOT loses to FLOT and PWC on all six metrics. The ranking mixes the method with the number of points.
Watch out

At a blur of 0.02, Sinkhorn’s iterations converge slowly. Like practical solvers, the lab lowers the blur step by step and stops after about 100 iterations; it does not reach the exact entropic optimum. Compared with a fully converged solver (POT, snippet 8), the lab’s balanced plan misplaces 1.3% of the mass and its robust plan transports 92% of the mass instead of 98%; individual displacements differ by up to 0.04. The conclusions do not change: with 3,000 iterations instead of 20 at the final blur, the errors of the table move by at most 0.006 and keep their order (for instance 0.0086 becomes 0.0085, and 0.0424 becomes 0.0437).

§3 Should we learn our graphs? p. 57–72 · fr. 48–62

§3.1 Dynamic graphs and autoencoders p. 58–59 · fr. 48–49

Dynamic graph CNNs (p. 58). “At every layer, use the K-NN graph of the feature vectors. This may promote semantic neighborhoods.” In DGCNN (Wang et al. 2019), the first layer connects each point of a cloud to its K nearest points in space, but later layers connect it to its K nearest points in the space of the current features. The slide’s figure shows airplanes coloured by the distance in feature space to one red point: in the first layer, the distance is roughly the distance in space; in deeper layers, both wing tips light up together although they are far apart.

Embeddings and autoencoders (p. 59). “Use the K-NN graph of a low-dimensional representation: UMAP, an encoder-decoder architecture…” An autoencoder compresses an image (the slide shows a handwritten 2 from François Chollet’s Keras tutorial) into a short code, then reconstructs it; the code is a representation in which neighbours can be sought. A linear autoencoder with a k-dimensional code, trained to minimise the squared reconstruction error, learns the same subspace as principal component analysis with k components (Baldi and Hornik 1989), so PCA is the simplest encoder of this kind.

The catch. A graph built from features is only as good as the features. With good features, neighbours share a meaning; with poor ones, they share a pixel pattern or nothing at all. And features that encode meaning usually come from labels, which are expensive (§3.3). Lab 9 builds the K-NN graph of the same MNIST images in six representations and measures how often neighbours share a label.

Lab 9

Neighbourhoods in feature space (p. 58–59)

Question. The same 1,000 images, six representations: raw pixels, three PCA codes, a UMAP layout, and a supervised projection. In which one do neighbours most often show the same digit?

Each image drawn as its digit
Label purity of the K-NN graph (share of the 10 nearest neighbours with the same digit) and leave-one-out 1-NN accuracy
What the lab shows (1,000 MNIST training images; PCA fitted on them without labels; discriminant analysis fitted on 4,000 other labelled images)
  • Pixels are already a decent space. Among the 10 nearest neighbours of an image in pixel space, 77.9% show the same digit (chance: 10.0%), and the single nearest neighbour does in 88.3% of cases.
  • A good low-dimensional code keeps the neighbourhoods. The 50 principal components do as well as the 784 pixels (79.5% purity, 88.5% for the nearest neighbour), and UMAP keeps 79.1% purity in only 2 dimensions, where the first 2 principal components keep 38.9%.
  • Labels help, but not in 2D. A projection fitted with labels on 4,000 other images (Fisher’s discriminant analysis) gives the purest graph, 81.7% with 9 directions, but only 41.1% with 2: ten classes need more than two linear directions.
  • Graphs follow features. The unsupervised UMAP layout is nearly as pure as the supervised 9-direction projection. This is the bet of p. 58–59: a better representation gives more “semantic” neighbourhoods. The table also shows its limit: the neighbourhoods are only as good as the features, and no representation here passes 82%.

§3.2 Attention layers and transformers p. 60–62 · fr. 50–52

Sentences are not grids (p. 60). “We would like to define convolutional architectures on sentences. But the 1D structure of the text is not always relevant.” In “The FBI is chasing a criminal on the run.”, the example of Cheng, Dong and Lapata (2016), the words that belong together, FBI and criminal, chasing and run, are several positions apart, and a window of fixed width either misses them or mixes in everything between.

Learn the neighbourhoods (p. 61). “Instead, we embed feature vectors in a semantic space. Attention = data-driven embedding + convolution. Transformer = stack of attention layers.” In the drawing, FBI and criminal land close together, and so do chasing and run: the neighbourhoods are defined by the learned embedding, as in DGCNN, but with soft weights instead of a hard K-NN graph.

The formula (p. 62). “Cheap and expressive convolution on the feature vectors xi: Query vectors qi ← MLPq(xi). Key vectors ki ← MLPk(xi). Value vectors vi ← MLPv(xi). Nadaraya–Watson interpolation with a kernel k(x, y) = exp(x · y):”

\[ \text{x}_\text{i} \;\gets\; \frac{\sum_\text{j} \exp(\text{q}_\text{i}\cdot\text{k}_\text{j})\,\text{v}_\text{j}}{\sum_\text{j} \exp(\text{q}_\text{i}\cdot\text{k}_\text{j})} \]

“This architecture trains remarkably well on web-scale corpuses.” The weights exp(qi · kj)/Σj exp(qi · kj) are the softmax of the scores qi · kj. This is exactly Lecture 2’s Nadaraya–Watson estimator (L2 §6.2): a weighted average of the values, with weights given by a kernel between the query and each key.

The author’s script. The figure of p. 62 is not a drawing: it is the output of code/regression.py, which runs Nadaraya–Watson with the kernel exp(γ x · y) on Lecture 2’s 2D toy data, for γ = 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000. The slide’s picture is byte for byte the file for γ = 50. The circles are the 20 training points, coloured by their value; the crosses are 20 other points of the same random generator (seed 2) that the script draws but never uses.

Key idea

The kernel exp(q · k) is not a “similarity decreasing with distance” like the Gaussian kernels of Lecture 2. Expanding \(\|\text{q}-\text{k}\|^2 = \|\text{q}\|^2 - 2\,\text{q}\cdot\text{k} + \|\text{k}\|^2\) gives

\[ \exp(\gamma\,\text{q}\cdot\text{k}) \;=\; \underbrace{\exp\!\big(\tfrac{\gamma}{2}\|\text{q}\|^2\big)}_{\text{cancels in the ratio}}\;\cdot\;\underbrace{\exp\!\big(-\tfrac{\gamma}{2}\|\text{q}-\text{k}\|^2\big)}_{\text{Gaussian kernel}}\;\cdot\;\underbrace{\exp\!\big(\tfrac{\gamma}{2}\|\text{k}\|^2\big)}_{\text{bias towards long keys}}. \]
\[ \begin{aligned} & \exp(\gamma\,\text{q}\cdot\text{k}) \\ &\quad = \exp\!\big(\tfrac{\gamma}{2}\|\text{q}\|^2\big) && \text{(cancels)} \\ &\quad\;\cdot\; \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{\gamma}{2}\|\text{q}-\text{k}\|^2\big) && \text{(Gaussian)} \\ &\quad\;\cdot\; \exp\!\big(\tfrac{\gamma}{2}\|\text{k}\|^2\big) && \text{(long keys)} \end{aligned} \]

The first factor depends on the query only and cancels between numerator and denominator. So dot-product attention is a Gaussian Nadaraya–Watson estimator of width \(1/\sqrt{\gamma}\) in which each key is given an extra weight \(\exp(\gamma\|\text{k}\|^2/2)\). When all keys have the same length (as normalisation layers roughly ensure), the extra weight is constant and attention is exactly a Gaussian kernel smoother. When they do not, long keys win: as γ grows, the weight concentrates on the key with the largest q · k, which is the key furthest in the direction of q, not the key nearest to q. (Transformers divide the scores by \(\sqrt{d}\), the dimension of the keys; in the formula of the slide this factor can be absorbed into the MLPs, and here it is the role of γ.)

Lab 10

Attention is a Nadaraya–Watson interpolator (p. 60–62)

Question. What does the kernel exp(γ x · y) of p. 62 do on Lecture 2’s toy data, and how does it differ from a Gaussian kernel of the same sharpness?

Prediction on the square [−0.5, 0.5]² (red = low, blue = high, as in the script’s colour map)
Mean |prediction − y| at the training points (the numbers the author’s script prints)
What the lab shows (default: the slide’s figure, 2D data, γ = 50, dot-product kernel)
  • The slide’s figure is reproduced. This page’s Nadaraya–Watson estimator with the kernel exp(γ x · y) gives the ten training errors printed by the author’s script (0.3353 at γ = 1 down to 0.2312 at γ = 20, then up to 0.4607 at γ = 1000) to within 6×10⁻¹⁷, and the map for γ = 50 matches the slide.
  • It is not a nearest-neighbour smoother. The heaviest weight goes to the nearest training point on only 49.0% of the square, whatever γ; with the Gaussian kernel it always does. Long keys are favoured: at γ = 50 the extra factor exp(γ|xj|²/2) ranges from 1.03 to 520 across the 20 points.
  • Sharpening does not interpolate. As γ grows, the Gaussian kernel’s training error falls towards 0 (0.038 at γ = 1000). The dot-product kernel’s error is smallest at γ = 20 and then grows, because all the weight goes to the training point furthest in the query’s direction. As γ → ∞, only 5 of the 20 points ever win: the corners of their convex hull (points 1, 7, 8, 13 and 16). The map freezes into 5 sectors.
  • In 1D the effect is stark. With the 9 points of Lecture 2, the dot-product kernel predicts, for large γ, the value of the rightmost point for every x > 0 and of the leftmost point for every x < 0. This is why attention layers normalise their inputs and learn the queries and keys: the raw kernel does not measure closeness.

§3.3 Three problems with learning everything p. 63–65 · fr. 53–55

Problem 1: data is expensive and fragmented (p. 63). “The Web and the Amazon Mechanical Turk are the exceptions, not the rule: 1 protein structure in 3D = months of work for a biologist. 50 fully documented patients = a great thesis for a radiologist. 1 patient in a clinical trial ≃ $40k, up to $1M for surgery! Getting legal access to large datasets and computers is extremely difficult in any field that has a signficant [sic] societal impact.” Lab 6 shows the scale of the difference: with 50 training images, the nearest-neighbour vote on MNIST is right about 6 times in 10; the networks of p. 35 were trained on 55,000.

Problem 2: bigger models are slower, heavier and cumbersome (p. 64). “We must strike a balance between: Speed. Accuracy. Hardware and development costs. Energy consumption = battery life. Interpretability = easy to debug = easy to maintain. Tons of equations ≃ Tons of parameters. Only worth the trouble if there is no other option.” The photograph of a chemical plant makes the point: a large model, like a large plant, has to be run, maintained and paid for.

Problem 3: in mature fields, structure is key to generalise (p. 65). A soldier fires a cannon; nine dots mark the ball’s flight towards a target. “This is especially true in fields that are close to physics, robotics… Fitting piecewise linear functions to parabolas or exponentials is fine for interpolation, but very limiting for extrapolation.” A ReLU network is piecewise linear (L2 §4.2): beyond the last data point it continues along a straight line, whatever the physics says. Gravity says parabola. Lab 11 digitises the slide’s dots and asks each model to hit the target.

Lab 11

Interpolation is not extrapolation (p. 47, 65)

Question. Shown the first part of the cannonball’s flight, which models predict where it lands? And what does a physical prior add when the data are noisy?

What the lab shows (default: the cannonball, the first 6 of its 10 dots seen, no noise)
  • Three parameters beat two hidden layers. Seeing the first 6 of the 10 dots, the parabola lands within 0.3 pixels of the target (fitted to the first 9 dots, it passes within 0.5 px of each of them), while the ReLU network misses by 69.7 px: past the data it continues in a straight line. With only 4 dots the parabola misses by 1.9 px and the network by 72.7 px; the network still misses by 5.8 px with 9 of the 10 dots.
  • Beware of lucky numbers. The Gaussian kernel ridge seems to hit the target with 6 dots (+0.5 px), but only because far from the data it falls back to the mean of the dots seen, 155.7 px, and the target happens to sit at 156 px. With 7 and 8 dots it misses by 9.2 and 15.3 px, and on the intermediate dots it is off by up to 19 px.
  • Growth is worse. On an exponential, the log-linear fit is exact from 4 points, while the ReLU network and the kernel underestimate the final value (441) by 238 and 353 with 6 points.
  • A prior is not a guarantee. With 5 px of noise and 6 dots, even the parabola misses by 46 px: three parameters estimated from the rising half of the flight are sensitive to noise. Adding a ReLU correction to the parabola (a miniature of Rosetta’s hybrid, p. 47) helps when the noise is small (2 px, 5 dots: −2.4 instead of −9.0 px) but can learn the noise (5 px, 8 dots: +43.3 instead of −4.4 px). Data-driven residuals need data too.

§3.4 A spectrum of fields, and careers p. 66–72 · fr. 56–62

A continuous spectrum of scientific fields (p. 66). Two axes, “Lots of maths” and “Lots of data”. High on maths and low on data: astrophysics, chemistry. Low on both: economy, history. High on data: board games, video games, natural images, natural language, highlighted as a band. A yellow ellipse joins biology images, medical images and natural images. “‘The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences’ and ‘the bitter lesson of AI’ apply to different ends of this spectrum.” The first phrase is the title of Eugene Wigner’s 1960 essay: laws written in mathematics predict far beyond the data that suggested them. The second is Richard Sutton’s 2019 essay: in AI, general methods that scale with computation have repeatedly beaten methods built on human knowledge. Each is true where it was observed; medical imaging sits in between.

Raw performance does not tell the whole story (p. 67). “Electric bikes travel at 30 km/h. Private jets travel at 800 km/h. Rockets travel at 30,000 km/h.” Nobody takes a rocket to work: the right tool depends on cost, energy and purpose, not on the top speed. “Monopolies claim that ‘bigger is better’.”

Choose your own path (p. 68–72). Insects that each found their own niche (an orchid mantis, a monarch butterfly, weaver ants, bees) face moths circling a light bulb. A 2016 quote of Geoffrey Hinton: “We should stop training radiologists now. It’s just completely obvious that within five years, deep learning is going to do better than radiologists.” A frame of DeepMind’s recruitment video (“Our mission is solving intelligence to advance science and benefit humanity”), under the title “Tech companies want you to forget that targeting ads ≠ solving cancer”. A cloud of problems for 2020–2050: quantum computers, chess engine++, efficient batteries, killer drones, automated MRI screening, autonomous cars, nuclear fusion, targeted ads, drug safety, protein design, efficient rail network, machine translation. “The French education system is giving you genuine freedom of choice. Use it wisely.” And an ikigai diagram: what you love, what you are good at, what the world needs, what you can be paid for.

Beyond the slides

These slides are advice, not results, and the page leaves them as such. Two facts can be added. Hinton’s five years ended in 2021, and radiologists are still being trained. And Wigner and Sutton are not in the slides’ bibliography; their essays are listed with the further references. The lab that fits this part best is Lab 11: on the cannonball, the piece of mathematics (a parabola) needs four points to predict the landing, and the model with the most parameters does worst.

What the slides conclude · references

The deck has no summary slide. Its three parts each end on a verdict. On the field: “Keep track of both classical and learning-based baselines … It is likely that the wave of papers on geometric deep learning will fade in most applications settings, and stick in some productive niches” (p. 39). On the author’s projects: “how far we can go if we drop complex physical terms but preserve the symmetries of the problem … Always stay humble” (p. 48), and “get the best of both data-driven and deterministic methods. Tables of numbers look impressive – but can hide critical information” (p. 56). On learning everything: “Tons of equations ≃ Tons of parameters. Only worth the trouble if there is no other option” (p. 64), and “Raw performance metrics do not tell the whole story” (p. 67). The last slides are advice on careers: “Find your own balance” (p. 72).

What to keep from this page. The labs confirm the slides’ technical claims and sharpen them. Isotropic message passing really cannot detect oriented edges (Lab 1), and a sphere really cannot carry a global direction (Lab 2). A layer that only sees the graph depends on the sampling (Lab 3), and a bridge of negative curvature throttles what reaches the other side (Lab 4). Irregular memory access costs several times more memory traffic, though much of it can be recovered by storing nearby vertices together (Lab 5). The claims about baselines hold up with numbers: a nearest-neighbour vote rivals the graph networks of p. 35 (Lab 6), optimal transport registers vessels without training (Lab 8), and a three-parameter law extrapolates where a network cannot (Lab 11). Two claims needed qualifying: RobOT’s win on KITTI depends on comparing 30,000 points against 8,000, and the ×100–×1,000 speed-up of dMaSIF includes MaSIF’s one-off pre-processing.

  15. Morton. A computer oriented geodetic data base and a new technique in file sequencing. IBM, 1966 (the Z-order curve). (Lab 5)
  16. Nadaraya. On estimating regression. Theory of Probability and its Applications, 9(1):141–142, 1964; and Watson. Smooth regression analysis. Sankhyā A, 26(4):359–372, 1964. (§3.2)
  17. Nocedal and Wright. Numerical optimization, 2nd edition, Springer, 2006 (L-BFGS and the strong Wolfe line search). (Lab 11)
  18. Sharp, Attaiki, Crane and Ovsjanikov. DiffusionNet: discretization agnostic learning on surfaces. ACM Transactions on Graphics, 41(3), 2022. (§1.5)
  19. Sutton. The bitter lesson. incompleteideas.net, 2019. (§3.4)
  20. Sverrisson, Feydy, Correia and Bronstein. Fast end-to-end learning on protein surfaces. CVPR, 15272–15281, 2021; code at github.com/FreyrS/dMaSIF (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), from which Lab 7 takes its parameters.
